questions.q: A vertical aerial photograph was taken with a camera of focal length 152 mm from a flying height of 2500 m above mean sea level. If the average terrain elevation is 500 m above mean sea level, what is the representative fraction (RF) scale of the photograph for the average terrain?
questions.a: Correct answer: 1:13,158 (or 1/13,158). Calculation: S = f / (H - h) = 152 mm / (2500 m - 500 m) = 152 mm / 2000 m = 152 mm / 2,000,000 mm = 1 / 13,158. A wrong answer reveals the student either forgot to convert units (mm to m), used H instead of (H - h), or inverted the fraction. This shows confusion between flying height above sea level and flying height above ground level.

questions.q: On a vertical aerial photograph, the distance between two road intersections measures 8.5 cm. The same distance measured on a 1:50,000 topographical map is 4.2 cm. What is the scale of the photograph? Explain why this method works even without knowing the focal length or flying height.
questions.a: Correct answer: Photograph scale = 1:24,706. Working: Map distance = 4.2 cm at 1:50,000 → Ground distance = 4.2 × 50,000 = 210,000 cm = 2.1 km. Photo distance = 8.5 cm for same ground distance → Photo scale = 8.5 / 210,000 = 1 / 24,706. This method works because both the photograph and map represent the same ground distance; the ratio of photo distance to map distance equals the inverse ratio of their scales. A wrong answer indicates the student cannot work across representations (photo ↔ map ↔ ground) or misapplies the scale conversion.

questions.q: A vertical aerial photograph covers a rectangular area 23 cm × 23 cm (photo format). The flying height above ground is 3000 m and focal length is 152 mm. Calculate the ground coverage (in km²) of this photograph. Then explain how the ground coverage would change if the same photograph were taken over mountainous terrain with 1000 m relief variation.
questions.a: Correct answer: Scale = 152 mm / 3,000,000 mm = 1:19,737. Photo side = 23 cm = 230 mm. Ground side = 230 mm × 19,737 = 4,539,510 mm = 4.54 km. Ground coverage = 4.54 × 4.54 = 20.6 km². Over mountainous terrain: scale varies across photo. For valley floor (h lower), flying height above ground increases → scale denominator increases → ground coverage per photo increases. For hilltops (h higher), flying height above ground decreases → scale denominator decreases → ground coverage per photo decreases. A wrong answer shows inability to convert photo dimensions to ground dimensions or misunderstanding of how relief affects scale variation.

questions.q: Two vertical aerial photographs of the same area are taken: Photo A at 3000 m above MSL with 152 mm focal length, Photo B at 6000 m above MSL with 304 mm focal length. The terrain elevation is 500 m. Compare the scales of the two photographs. Are they identical? Justify your answer mathematically and explain the practical implication for photo interpretation.
questions.a: Correct answer: Yes, scales are identical. Photo A: S = 152 / (3000 - 500) = 152 / 2500 = 1:16,447. Photo B: S = 304 / (6000 - 500) = 304 / 5500 = 1:18,092. Wait - these are NOT identical! Let me recalculate: 152/2500 = 0.0608, 304/5500 = 0.0553. They differ. The student must recognize that doubling both focal length and flying height does NOT preserve scale because the terrain elevation (500 m) is subtracted from flying height. The ratio f/(H-h) changes unless h=0. Practical implication: You cannot simply "zoom in" by increasing focal length and altitude proportionally; terrain elevation breaks the proportionality. A wrong answer reveals the student treats the formula as a simple proportion without considering the subtractive effect of ground elevation.

questions.q: A surveyor needs to produce a 1:10,000 scale orthophoto map of a floodplain (elevation 200 m) using a camera with 152 mm focal length. The aircraft can fly at 2000 m, 2500 m, or 3000 m above MSL. Which flying height should be chosen? Evaluate the trade-offs if the surveyor chooses 3000 m instead of the optimal height.
questions.a: Correct answer: Required H - h = f / S = 152 mm / (1/10,000) = 152 mm × 10,000 = 1,520,000 mm = 1520 m. So H = 1520 + 200 = 1720 m above MSL. None of the given heights match exactly; 2000 m is closest (gives scale 1:11,846). Choosing 3000 m gives scale = 152 / (3000 - 200) = 1:18,421 — too small scale (less detail). Trade-offs: Higher altitude → smaller scale → larger ground coverage per photo (fewer photos needed, lower cost) but reduced ground resolution (cannot see small features like drainage channels, individual trees). For floodplain mapping requiring detailed drainage analysis, 3000 m is unsuitable. A poor evaluation ignores the resolution requirement or miscalculates the scale.

questions.q: Design a field procedure to determine the scale of an old vertical aerial photograph (no camera metadata available) of the Yamuna floodplain near Delhi. You have access to a current 1:25,000 topographical map of the area and GPS equipment. List the steps, identify potential error sources, and explain how you would validate your result.
questions.a: Expected answer: Steps: (1) Identify 8-10 clearly recognizable, unchanged features (road intersections, building corners, bridge ends) on both photo and map. (2) Measure photo distances (mm) between feature pairs using a stereoscope or high-resolution scan. (3) Measure corresponding map distances (cm) and convert to ground distances using map scale. (4) Calculate scale for each pair: S_i = photo_dist_i / ground_dist_i. (5) Compute mean scale and standard deviation. (6) Validate: Use GPS to measure 3-4 ground control points not used in calculation; compare photo-predicted positions with GPS positions. Error sources: Feature misidentification (changes over time), map measurement error, photo distortion (relief displacement), paper shrinkage/expansion. Validation criterion: Mean positional error < 2 mm on photo (equivalent to < 50 m ground at 1:25,000). A poor answer omits validation, uses too few points, or ignores relief displacement effects.
